svg.title: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead of taking anyone's word for it: The toolbox tells a real failure apart from a run that died on its way to the test
svg.text: The toolbox checks the test really failed first, instead
of taking anyone's word for it
Scenario: The toolbox tells a real failure apart from a run that died on its way to the test
The phase refuses to certify itself

g.text: Given a developer writes the test for a greeting the toolbox cannot give yet
A developer starts a new feature the honest way: the test first. The terminal shows, as git sees them, the two new files
and the one line that registers the step file with the test suite.
The test asks for a greeting the toolbox cannot give yet, so it is meant to fail. But look at the second line of the
step file: it also asks for a helper file, ../helpers/greeting, that nobody has written yet.
Then the run dies on its way to the test, exits like a failed test, and the toolbox refuses
to call that a proof
One typed line does the whole check: what git sees, the test run, its exit code, the report folder, then the toolbox's
check. The run is the line task project:test:e2e runs inside its test container.
The run never reaches the test. Node stops on "Cannot find module '../helpers/greeting'", the toolbox's wrapper reports
"Worker completion: FAIL", and the exit code is 1, the code a failed test returns. At a glance, this looks like the
proof the method asks for.
The report folder does not even exist, because nothing ran. The check reads that folder and refuses: "The run left no
report at all: it stopped before a single scenario ran."
When the developer writes the missing helper, the test fails on its own check, and the
toolbox accepts that failure as proof
The developer writes the missing helper, and nothing else: git now lists helpers/greeting.js next to the test, which is
untouched. The greeting the test asks for still does not exist.
Same line as the card before. This time the suite reaches the test and fails on its own check: "expected 'Hello,
Lambda', got ''". The engine prints that failure twice, once for its worker and once for the whole run, and the report
folder now holds results-1.xml, the record of that one scenario.
The verdict has turned: "The failure is real: the scenario ran and failed on its own check", and it quotes that check.
Nobody had to be believed: the proof was on disk, and the toolbox read it.
Then a run that selects no scenario wipes that report, and the toolbox refuses the old
failure
The report of the card before is still on disk: the first ls lists results-1.xml. The developer runs the suite again
with a typo in the tag, and @greting selects no scenario at all.
The run stops at once: "No Gherkin scenario matches this selection", exit code 1. The toolbox emptied the report folder
before anything else, so the second ls finds nothing.
Asked about @greeting again, the same check now refuses. The failure it accepted a minute ago went away with its report:
only the latest run counts as proof.
Then the test phase refuses to certify itself, the moment a check is switched off
Asked to make the suite green, the assistant takes the cheapest road: one word, @skip, above the scenario it could not
satisfy. The file on screen is the test as it now stands.
task devsecops:test:verify is the one command that certifies the test phase: the tests passed, and nothing was switched
off to get there. Its guard runs first, so it stops in a second instead of after the whole test suite.
It names the file, the line and what that line does, then offers the only way past it: a No-cheat-exempt trailer in the
commit, so a reviewer reads the reason instead of guessing it.
